podcast.body: This song was a big hit for Jerry Lee Lewis. During a Boston concert in 1958, police prevented the audience from dancing to it, causing them to be seated and squirming, unable to fully engage with the performance. "Lewis had had to play his set to an audience who was seated and squirming, unable to get up and dance to his recent big hit, like Great Bulls of Fire."

podcast.body: This song was immediately recognized as a hit by Lewis and Sam Phillips upon hearing Otis Blackwell's demo. Phillips was concerned about how to improve upon Blackwell's nearly perfect demo. It was tailored specifically for Lewis's established persona, refining the "Whole Lotta Shakin'" formula with a more dynamic, stop-start opening. A film version was quickly cut for "Jamboree," but several days were spent perfecting the hit record, focusing on the intro. Lewis expressed theological concerns about the song sounding "satanic," leading to an angry discussion with Phillips, who eventually persuaded him to continue recording. Released with Hank Williams' "You Win Again" as the B-side, it was an immediate success, selling over a million copies in the first ten days and becoming a classic that defines 1950s Rock and Roll. It established Lewis as one of the genre's greatest stars and has been covered by artists from Dolly Parton to Aerosmith. "It's one of the records that defines 1950s Rock and Roll music, and it firmly established Jerry Lee Lewis as one of the greatest stars of Rock and Roll, if not the greatest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
